source_text: Iam nunc putas delectamentis L exige re spatium hoc? cur tam ingratus es, ut tot et tales uoluptates a deo contributas tibi satis non habeas neque recognoscas? quid enim incundius quam dei patris et domini reconciliatio, quam ueritatis reuelatio, quam errorum recognitio, quam tantorum retro criminum uenia? quae maior uoluptas quam fastidium ipsius uoluptatis, quam saeculi totius contemptus, quam uera libertas, quam conscientia integra, quam uita sufficiens, quam mortis timor nullus ? quod calcas deos nationum, quod daemonia expellis, quod medicinas facis, quod reuelationes petis, quod deo uiuis? haec uoluptates, haec spectacula Christianorum sancta perpetua gratuita; in his tibi circenses ludos interpretare, cursus saeculi intuere, tempora labentia, spatia peracta dinumera, metas consummationis exspecta, societates ecclesiarum defende, ad signum dei suscitare, ad tubain angeli erigere, ad martyrum palmas gloriare. si scaenicae doctrinae delectant, satis nobis litterarum est, satis uersuum est, satis sententiarum, satis etiam canticorum, satis uocum, nec fabulae, sed ueritates, nec strophae, sed simplicitates. uis et pugilatus et luctatus? praesto sunt, non parua et multa. aspice impudicitiam deiectam a castitate, perfidiam Caesam a fide, saeuitiam a misericordia contusam, petulantiam a modestia adumbratam, et tales sunt apud nos agones, in quibus ipsi coronamur. uis autem et sanguinis aliquid? habes Christi.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing the Christian reader directly, urging them to find their entertainment in the spiritual blessings and moral victories of the Christian life rather than in the public shows.
pass_a_gloss: Do you now think that I should demand space for these delights? Why are you so ungrateful that you do not consider the so many and such great pleasures contributed to you by God as enough, and do not recognize them? For what is more pleasant than reconciliation with God the Father and Lord, than the revelation of truth, than the recognition of errors, than the pardon of so many past crimes? What greater pleasure is there than disgust with pleasure itself, than contempt of the whole world, than true freedom, than a clean conscience, than a sufficient life, than no fear of death? What greater pleasure is there than that you trample on the gods of the nations, that you cast out demons, that you perform healings, that you seek revelations, that you live for God? These are the pleasures, these are the shows of Christians: holy, everlasting, free of charge. In these interpret for yourself the circus games: look at the course of the world, the slipping-away times, count up the completed laps, await the turning-post of the consummation, defend the fellowship of the churches, be roused at the signal of God, be raised up at the trumpet of the angel, glory in the palms of the martyrs. If the teachings of the stage delight you, we have enough of literature, enough of verses, enough of maxims, enough also of songs, enough of voices, and not fables but truths, not tricks but simplicities. Do you want also boxing and wrestling? They are at hand, not small and many. Look at shamelessness cast down by chastity, faithlessness slain by faith, cruelty bruised by mercy, wantonness overshadowed by modesty, and such are the contests among us, in which we ourselves are crowned. Do you want also something of blood? You have the blood of Christ.

choices.why: The brief's glossary bans 'enjoyment' for uoluptas; 'delights' keeps the plural noun force of the Latin and matches the rhetorical contrast with the shows.
The brief's glossary requires 'pleasure' for uoluptas, and the plural here is rendered as 'pleasures' to preserve the plural force.
The brief's glossary requires 'shows' for spectacula, and the phrase 'shows of Christians' preserves the paradox Tertullian is making.
The brief's glossary gives 'circus' for circus and 'games' for ludi; rendering the phrase as 'circus games' keeps both terms distinct and literal.
Meta is the turning-post in the circus; 'turning-post' preserves the circus metaphor while 'consummation' renders consummatio literally.
Stropha means a trick or artifice, especially in theatrical or rhetorical contexts; 'tricks' keeps the contrast with 'truths' sharp.

pass_b_english: Do you really think you need this space for delights? Why are you so ungrateful that you do not count as enough the many great pleasures God has contributed to you, and do not even recognize them? What is more joyful than reconciliation with God the Father and Lord, than the revelation of truth, than the recognition of errors, than pardon for so many past crimes? What greater pleasure is there than disgust at pleasure itself, than contempt for the whole world, than true freedom, than a clean conscience, than a life that is sufficient, than no fear of death? What of trampling the gods of the nations, expelling demons, working cures, seeking revelations, living for God? These are the pleasures, these are the shows of Christians—holy, everlasting, free. In these, interpret the circus games for yourself: gaze at the course of the world, the slipping seasons, count out the laps already run, wait for the turning-post of the consummation, defend the fellowship of the churches, rise at God's signal, stand at the angel's trumpet, glory in the martyrs' palms. If the theater's teachings delight you, we have literature enough, verses enough, sayings enough, songs enough, voices enough—not fables but truths, not tricks but simplicities. Do you want boxing and wrestling too? They are at hand, and they are not small or few. Look at impurity thrown down by chastity, faithlessness slain by faith, cruelty crushed by mercy, wantonness overshadowed by modesty. Such are the contests among us, in which we ourselves win the crown. Do you want some blood as well? You have Christ's.
